Plus, CoreWeave’s mixed signal, and OpenAi’s mounting losses
 

Good morning, I’m filling in for Spencer Jakab. Stocks are poised to open on an upbeat note following CoreWeave’s results, which served to relieve immediate angst about the AI trade. Nvidia’s shares, which have been pummeled in recent days over CEO Jensen Huang’s affair, look set to rebound sharply along with other chip and data-center stocks. Oil has stopped its recent skid, and the U.S. Treasury market is closed in observance of Veterans Day.

Capitol pill

 

Hospitals are the costliest part of America’s healthcare system. So with Democrats taking over Congress and promising lower healthcare costs, you’d think hospital executives would be worried.

 

Quite the opposite. Shares of HCA Healthcare, Universal Health Services and Tenet Healthcare are all up sharply since the election.

 

A big reason is coverage. Both parties promise affordable healthcare. But since neither side has managed to rein in costs, they’re really fighting about who gets insured.

 

Republicans cut Medicaid in last year’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act and let enhanced Obamacare subsidies lapse. Democrats want both moves reversed. For hospitals, that’s the whole game: An uninsured patient who shows up at the ER still gets treated, but often can’t pay.

 

With Democrats running Capitol Hill, hospitals can count on no further cuts and even hope to see some reversed. Many analysts expect President Trump to veto any such attempt.

 

Still, the size of the Democratic wave makes a healthcare trade possible. As long as it is, hospital stocks could maintain their momentum.

 

Ipsita Smolinski of Capitol Street thinks there’s a chance Trump could agree to restore subsidies and even delay Medicaid work requirements. He could do so in exchange for drug-pricing wins, such as writing his “most-favored-nation” deals with drugmakers into law. 

 

A more plausible, and even bigger, prize involves a money machine hospitals have come to rely on, but could soon face curbs.

 

For years, states have taxed hospitals to help finance their share of Medicaid spending, using the money to draw down additional federal funds. They then channel some of that money back to hospitals through supplemental payments.

 

It’s a bit like handing over one candy and getting two back. These payments have become an important source of hospital profits. Trump’s tax law pressures both the financing mechanism and the payments themselves, with major changes beginning in 2028.

 

Many Democrats oppose the cuts. And, because they are a ways off, there is time for a deal. Baird analyst Michael Ha puts the odds at better than even that Democrats win hospitals some relief.

 

The money is big. HCA gets around 15% to 20% of its earnings from these arrangements, Ha estimates. Universal Health Services gets an even bigger chunk. That helps explain why the latter’s stock has risen most among the big three, over 10%, since the midterms.

 

After the rally, hospital stocks trade above their historical average valuations, so investors are already paying up for that bet. But if relief comes, today’s earnings estimates, which assume no policy help, look low, and the stocks may not be as expensive as they appear, says Ha.

 

Betting on compromise in Washington is a brave thing to do. But having friends in power always beats the alternative. And, come January, hospitals will have a lot more of them.
